column1: # This repository's ideas, explained simply (lesson::eli5): id, the term, the explanation, a worked example, the demo that teaches it. MADE by scripts/glossary.py from docs/glossary.md, the one source: edit that file, then `just glossary`; the gate checks they agree.

column3: A space that is flat up close: look at a small enough piece of it and it is, as near as you like, an ordinary flat space of some dimension. The earth is round and the floor is flat, and both are true: the floor is a small piece of the earth. A circle is a manifold of one dimension, the skin of a ball one of two. Not every curved set is a manifold: a surface with a corner or an edge (a cube's skin, a polytope) is not flat at the corner, and here is not called one.
column4: On the sphere, two points a tenth of a radian apart are 0.1000 apart along it and 0.0999 straight through: nearly the same, as on a floor. Two points a quarter turn apart are 1.571 along it and 1.414 through: not the same.

column3: How many directions you can move in along a space: the number of coordinates its own map needs. An ant on the skin of a ball can go north or east, two directions, so the skin has intrinsic dimension two, whatever room it sits in. Not the number of coordinates of the room (that is the ambient dimension).
column4: The circle: one (its map is one angle). The sphere, the torus and the Swiss roll: two.

column3: The number of coordinates of the room a space is drawn in: how many numbers each point is written with. The skin of a ball drawn in a room of three coordinates has ambient dimension three and intrinsic dimension two; the difference is what makes it curved inside the room. Not the intrinsic dimension; the two agree only when the space is the room itself (the Poincare disk is drawn in its own two).
column4: A word embedding of 64 numbers has ambient dimension 64; if the words lie near a curved sheet of few directions, its intrinsic dimension is small.

column3: What makes a manifold a manifold, said as a measurement: between two points close together, the straight-line distance through the room and the shortest distance along the space nearly agree. Far apart, they do not.
column4: Swiss roll, points a and b a little apart round the sheet: 1.626 through the air, 1.633 along the sheet. Points a and c one turn apart: 6.28 through the air, 52.8 along the sheet.

column3: The shortest path between two points measured along a space, as against the straight line through the room around it: what the string pulled tight on the surface does. On a sphere it is an arc of a great circle, the route an airplane flies; on the Poincare disk, an arc of a circle meeting the rim at right angles, or a diameter. Not a straight line, except on a flat space.
column4: From p to r on the sphere, the geodesic is 0.873 long and the straight line (the chord through the inside) 0.518.

column3: The assumption that the points a model learns from, though written with many numbers, lie near a curved thing of few directions inside that room: a data manifold. It is an assumption made so that a method can be built on it, not a fact about every data set, and these pages call it one (the literature's "manifold hypothesis"). Not a statement that a learned representation is a single smooth manifold; it need not be.
column4: The Swiss roll: three numbers per point, two directions along the sheet.

column3: The curved thing a data set lies near, under the manifold assumption: the points themselves, in the room they are given in. Not a representation manifold, which is a space a model is made to put its points on by choice; the two are kept apart here, because an experiment can match one to the other or not.
column4: The Swiss roll is a data manifold; the sphere a classifier puts its unit-length representations on is a representation manifold.

column3: A shape with flat faces, straight edges and corners, like a cube or a diamond, in any number of dimensions: the set of points that satisfy some linear inequalities. The Birkhoff polytope is the set of doubly stochastic matrices of one size; its corners are the permutation matrices (Birkhoff, von Neumann). A polytope is flat in pieces but not locally flat at a corner or an edge, so it is not a smooth manifold and is not called one here: a method that stays inside one is "constrained to a polytope", not "on a manifold".
column4: The 3 by 3 doubly stochastic matrices: nine entries, four free, a polytope of dimension four with six corners (the six permutations).

column3: At a point of a manifold, a direction you can move in without leaving it, with a length: an arrow lying flat against the surface there. All such arrows at one point make its tangent space, a flat space of the manifold's intrinsic dimension: the floor the ant stands on. A vector of the room is made tangent by dropping its part that points off the surface. Not a point of the manifold: an arrow at a point.
column4: On the unit sphere at p = (1, 0, 0), the vector (2, 3, 0) has tangent part (0, 3, 0): its part along p is dropped.

column3: The rule that gives the length of a tangent vector, and so the distance between nearby points, at every point of a space: the ruler. Change the rule and the same points are different distances apart, the same step a different size. Not the distance function itself (which the metric determines) and not a norm on the whole room: it may differ from point to point, as the Poincare disk's ruler shrinks toward the rim.
column4: On the Poincare disk, a step of 0.035 on paper near the middle is 0.070 by the disk's ruler; the same step near the rim is 3.87.

column3: How a space departs from flat, measured by what happens to triangles and circles: on a flat space (curvature zero) a triangle's angles add to a half turn and a circle's circumference is 2 pi times its radius; on a sphere (positive) the angles add to more and circles are shorter; on a hyperbolic space (negative) the angles add to less and circles grow faster than their radius, exponentially so. A number per point, which can vary; here mostly one number for the whole space (the sphere's is 1, the Poincare disk's is -1, a plane's 0). Not the same as dimension or topology: a sphere and a torus both have intrinsic dimension two and different curvature and topology.
column4: The Poincare disk's ruler: the marks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 from the middle sit at 0.46, 0.76, 0.91, 0.96, 0.99 on paper.

column3: What is left of a shape when lengths and angles are forgotten and only connectedness remains: how many pieces it has, how many holes, whether a loop on it can be shrunk to a point. A sphere and a cube's skin have the same topology; a sphere and a torus do not (the torus has a hole). Not geometry: two spaces of the same topology can have different curvature and metric. A flow that can be run backward cannot change topology: it cannot tear one piece into two.
column4: A circle and a square are the same topologically; a circle and a line are not (cut the circle once and it is still one piece; the line is already two ends).

column3: Taking a step: from a point, along a tangent vector, staying on the manifold, for a distance equal to the vector's length. The exponential map is the exact step, along the geodesic (on the sphere: cos t p + sin t v / t). A retraction is any cheaper step that agrees with it for small vectors (on the sphere: add the vector and scale back to length 1). Its inverse, the arrow from one point to another, is the logarithmic map. Not an exponential of a number: the name is historical.
column4: From p = (1, 0, 0) along (0, pi/2, 0): a quarter turn, landing on (0, 1, 0).

column3: The point of the manifold whose summed squared distances along it to a set of points is least (the Frechet or Karcher mean): the average that stays on the space. The plain average of points on a sphere falls inside the sphere; the mean on the sphere is found by stepping repeatedly along the average of the arrows to the points, which cancel at the mean. Not the plain average put back on the space, which is a different point.
column4: Three points on the sphere (the axes): the plain mean is 0.42 inside; the mean on the sphere is their common direction.

column3: How badly a set of distances is kept when points are put into a space: for every pair, the ratio (or the difference) of the distance the space gives them to the distance they should have, summed or averaged over the pairs. Zero when every distance is kept. A tree's distances cannot be kept in a flat space of few dimensions (the number of nodes grows exponentially with depth); in a hyperbolic space they nearly can. Not a model's accuracy on a task: a representation can be accurate and distorted, or faithful and useless, and the two are measured apart.
column4: A tree of depth 4 embedded in the plane, on the sphere and in the Poincare disk at the same dimension: three distortion numbers, compared.

column3: A direction and a speed at every point of a space: an arrow drawn at each point, saying where a thing there would go next. Wind on a map is one. A state that follows the field traces a path, a trajectory. Not a single vector, and not a gradient field unless it comes from a potential.
column4: On the plane, the field (-y, x) turns every point round the origin: a rotation.

column3: A vector field that comes from a single function (the potential, in training the loss): at each point the arrow points the way the function rises fastest (its gradient), and following the arrows backward is gradient descent. Such a field cannot circle: going round a loop and coming back, the function is where it was. A general vector field need not come from any function; a pure rotation does not. Not every vector field is a gradient field, and that is why gradient descent and a flow are different things.
column4: The field (x, 3 y) is the gradient of (x^2 + 3 y^2) / 2; the rotation (-y, x) is the gradient of nothing.

column3: Two numbers that summarize a vector field at a point: the divergence says whether the field spreads out (positive) or draws in (negative) there; the curl says whether it turns, and which way. A gradient field has no curl; a rotation has no divergence. Not properties of a single arrow: they are about how the arrows change from point to point.
column4: The rotation (-y, x): divergence 0, curl 2 everywhere. The field (x, y): divergence 2, curl 0.

column3: A flow is the motion of every point under a vector field over time: where each starting point ends after a while. An integrator is the arithmetic that follows a field step by step from a start (Euler: one step along the arrow; Runge-Kutta: a weighted average of several looks ahead), with an error that depends on the step size and the method. Not the field itself: one field, many integrators, and they do not land in the same place.
column4: Following the rotation with Euler steps of 0.1 for one turn spirals outward; a fourth-order Runge-Kutta stays near the circle.

column3: A network whose layers are the steps of an integrator following a learned vector field: the same field applied again and again moves the representation from input to output. Then a question about the network is a question about the flow: where it carries points, what it cannot do (a flow run backward cannot tear a piece in two). Not a network with many different layers; one field, stepped.
column4: A small learned field carrying one set of points on the sphere to another, in five steps held to the sphere.

column3: The room of all the numbers a model can have: every setting of its weights is one point, and training moves that point. The loss is a function on this room, and the step of training is a step through it. Not the data's room and not the representation's: three different rooms, with three different geometries.
column4: A layer of 4 by 4 weights lives in a parameter space of 16 dimensions.

column3: The direction of steepest rise of a function on a manifold, measured by the manifold's own metric and lying in the tangent space: the ordinary gradient with its off-surface part dropped and its length corrected by the metric. The step then goes along it with the exponential map or a retraction, and stays on the manifold. Not the plain gradient followed by putting the point back, which is a retraction of a different vector.
column4: On the sphere, the gradient of a loss at p has its part along p removed; the step along it is cos t p + sin t v / t.

column3: A gradient step measured by the Fisher metric (Amari): instead of asking which change of the weights lowers the loss most per unit of weight change, ask which lowers it most per unit of change in what the model predicts. The step is the gradient multiplied by the inverse of the Fisher matrix. It can take fewer steps and costs more per step; whether it pays is measured, not assumed. Not a different loss: the same loss, a different ruler.
column4: A tiny model trained with plain gradient descent, a diagonal preconditioner and a natural-gradient approximation: loss by step and steps to a target, with the cost of each step counted.

column3: A matrix that reshapes a gradient step: the step is the gradient multiplied by it. The identity is plain gradient descent; a diagonal preconditioner scales each weight's step on its own (Adam's averages do this); the inverse Fisher matrix gives the natural gradient. A preconditioner is a choice of metric on the parameter space. Not a change of the loss or of the data.
column4: On the loss (x^2 + 3 y^2) / 2 the plain step zigzags down the narrow valley; the step under the metric diag(1, 1/3) goes straight.

column3: The set of transformations a model is allowed to use, chosen before training: all matrices with rows and columns summing to one, all orthogonal matrices, all matrices of rank at most r. Training is kept inside it by a projection or a parameterization. Some constraint sets are smooth manifolds (the orthogonal group), some are polytopes (the doubly stochastic matrices), some are stratified sets (rank at most r); the pages say which. Not the data manifold and not the parameter space: a subset of the parameter space, with its own shape.
column4: mHC keeps its mixing matrices doubly stochastic.

column3: A square matrix with no negative entries whose every row and every column sums to one. Multiplying a set of streams by one takes a weighted average of them, with the weights summing to one along both ways, so nothing is amplified: the size of the signal cannot grow (its largest singular value is at most one) and the mean of the streams is kept exactly. The set of such matrices is the Birkhoff polytope. Not a stochastic matrix (rows only) and not an orthogonal matrix (which may have negative entries and keeps lengths, not means).
column4: [[0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5]] averages two streams; the identity leaves them alone; both are doubly stochastic.

column3: A way to make a matrix of positive entries doubly stochastic: divide each row by its sum, then each column by its sum, and repeat; the row and column sums both tend to one (Sinkhorn 1964; Sinkhorn and Knopp 1967). Stopped early, the result is nearly doubly stochastic, and the pages measure how nearly (the row and column sum errors). It is also, in optimal transport, the fast way to a regularized transport plan (Cuturi 2013). Not an exact projection unless run to convergence; mHC runs twenty sweeps.
column4: From exp of a 3 by 3 table of logits, three sweeps bring the column sums within 0.01 of one; twenty within 1e-6, for a well-mixed start.

column3: The set of square matrices that keep every length and every angle: rotations and reflections. It is a smooth manifold (of dimension n(n - 1)/2 for n by n matrices), not a polytope; a step on it is kept on it by a retraction (the nearest orthogonal matrix, from the SVD). Mixing streams by an orthogonal matrix keeps the size of the signal exactly, at the price of negative entries: not an average. Not the doubly stochastic matrices, which keep means and not lengths.
column4: A rotation of the plane by 30 degrees; the identity; a swap of two streams (a permutation, which is both orthogonal and doubly stochastic).

column3: Two manifolds of frames and subspaces: the Stiefel manifold is the set of matrices with r orthonormal columns in n dimensions (a frame); the Grassmann manifold is the set of r-dimensional subspaces of an n-dimensional space (a frame with its basis forgotten: all frames spanning the same subspace are one point). The home of low-rank adapters' subspaces and shared bases. Not the set of matrices of rank at most r, which is not a manifold (a stratified set).
column4: A LoRA adapter's two thin matrices span a subspace of rank r: a point of a Grassmann manifold; changing the basis of the subspace moves the frame on the Stiefel manifold and not the point on the Grassmann manifold.

column2: stratified set (matrices of rank at most r)
column3: A set made of smooth pieces of different dimensions fitted together, like a cone with its tip: smooth away from the joins, not at them. The matrices of rank at most r are one: the matrices of rank exactly r form a smooth manifold, and the matrices of smaller rank sit inside as its edge, where it is not locally flat. A step that lowers the rank crosses a join. Not a smooth manifold, and not a polytope (it has no flat faces).
column4: The 2 by 2 matrices of rank at most 1: a cone in four dimensions whose tip is the zero matrix.

column3: The running vector a deep network passes from layer to layer, to which each layer adds its small change (the residual) instead of replacing it: x then x + f(x) then x + f(x) + g(x + f(x)). The stream is what makes very deep networks trainable: a layer that learns nothing passes the stream through unchanged. Not the layer's output alone; the layer's output added to what came in.
column4: A stack of 12 layers over a stream of 8 numbers: the size of the stream after each layer, forward, and the size of the gradient, backward.

column3: Several residual streams side by side instead of one (n copies of the hidden state), with a learned matrix mixing them at every layer and learned weights saying which streams a layer reads and writes (Zhu et al., ICLR 2025). Unconstrained, the mixing matrices multiplied through many layers can grow or shrink the signal by a large factor: the mHC paper measured a gain of about three thousand at 27B parameters. Not a wider layer: the same layer, several streams.
column4: Four streams of 8 numbers, a 4 by 4 mixing matrix per layer, free; the gain of the product of 12 of them.

column3: Hyper-connections with the mixing matrices kept doubly stochastic (DeepSeek, Dec 2025, ICML 2026): the mixing is then a weighted average of the streams, which cannot amplify the signal through any depth, and the mean of the streams is passed through exactly. The constraint is enforced by twenty Sinkhorn sweeps on the exponential of learned logits, so it is approximate (the composite gain measured about 1.6, not 1). The name says "manifold"; the set is the Birkhoff polytope, which these pages call a polytope.
column4: Four streams, mixing matrices from Sinkhorn: the gain through 12 layers stays near 1 where free mixing's drifts.

column3: The way a model keeps a point: the list of numbers that stands for it, and the space those numbers are read in. The same point can be kept as it is (a flat space, measured by the straight line) or as its direction only (a point of the unit sphere, measured by the angle). Which is chosen is a choice of geometry, made before anything is learned; not the data itself, which is the same under both.
column4: A direction of length 2 pointing up and right, kept flat, is (1.41, 1.41); kept on the sphere it is (0.71, 0.71), and its length is gone.

column3: The shortest way along the skin of a sphere between two of its points: along the circle cut by the plane through them and the middle, the way an airplane flies. For the unit sphere it is the angle between the two points, in radians, from 0 to pi; the straight line through the inside (the chord) is always shorter, 2 sin of half the angle. Not the cosine distance, though for unit points the two order neighbors the same way.
column4: Two points a quarter turn apart: 1.571 along the sphere, 1.414 straight through.

column3: One less the cosine of the angle between two points, where the cosine is their product summed over the coordinates divided by their two lengths: 0 for points that point the same way, 1 for points at right angles, 2 for opposite ones. It ignores the lengths, as the angle does, and orders pairs as the angle does, since the cosine only falls as the angle grows; it is not the angle, and is not a distance along any space.
column4: Two points at a quarter turn: cosine 0, cosine distance 1; at a tenth of a radian: cosine distance 0.005.

column3: The plainest way to classify: keep the training points with their labels, and for a new point find the k training points nearest it, under whichever distance was chosen, and answer with the label most of them have. It learns no number, so the distance is all the geometry it has; change the distance and the neighbors change. Not a trained model, though it is a classifier.
column4: With k = 5 and the straight line, a point whose five nearest are three of class 1 and two of class 2 is called class 1.

column3: The line (or surface) where a classifier changes its answer: on one side it says one class, on the other another. Drawn by asking the classifier at every point of a grid and coloring each by its answer. Under the straight line the boundary between two clusters is a line midway between them; under the angle it is a ray from the middle, since every point of a ray is the same direction.
column4: On the directions, the straight line's boundary moves when the point's length changes and the angle's does not; the page draws it at three lengths.

column3: Points set aside before training, never shown to the model, on which it is tested: the share of them it labels right is the held-out accuracy, the measure of what was learned rather than remembered. Here a seeded quarter of every set, the same quarter for every geometry compared. Not the training points, whose accuracy says only what was fitted.
column4: 120 points: 90 trained on, 30 held out; 27 of the 30 right is 0.9.

column3: The number a classifier is trained to lower: for each training point, minus the logarithm of the probability the model gives its true class, averaged over the points. 0 when every true class gets probability 1; log of the number of classes (1.10 for three, 1.39 for four) when the model guesses evenly. It falls as the model grows sure of the right answers; the held-out accuracy is measured apart.
column4: A model giving the true class probability 0.5 on every point has loss 0.69.

column3: What a model does when it keeps lowering its training loss by remembering its training points rather than by learning their structure: the training loss falls while the held-out accuracy stops rising or falls. More steps, or more numbers, make it likelier on a small set. Not a property of a geometry; a sign that a comparison of geometries must hold the steps and the numbers equal and look at the held-out figure.
column4: A loss that falls from 0.5 to 0.3 while the held-out accuracy goes from 0.75 to 0.675.

column3: Every figure on a page is marked one or the other. Measured: a number the X_eTaL program computed from a run (a distance between points it made, a loss after a step). Analytical: a shape drawn from its formula (the wire lines of a sphere), which the program also computed point by point, but which shows where a space is, not something learned or found. Not a claim about accuracy: a mark of what kind of thing a figure is.
column4: The sphere's parallels and meridians are analytical; the chord and the great-circle distance between p and q are measured.

column3: A run in which the geometry compared made no difference, or cost more and helped nothing. It is written up as a result like any other, with what would have counted for the hypothesis written before the run. Not a failure of the experiment: a finding about the geometry.
column4: If the hierarchical data embeds no better in the disk than in the plane at the same dimension, the H1 table says so.

column3: The three questions of this repository, each with its test, its measures and what would count against it written before any run (docs/research-questions.md): H1, a geometry that matches the data's structure helps a representation; H2, a constraint on a transformation keeps a deep network stable; H3, geometry learned with the model can beat geometry chosen for it on mixed tasks, and can also deceive.
column4: Each explorer's page names the hypothesis its demo bears on, in its `demo.toml`.
